title: Latency onset curvebook by cold-warm flow
content:
Purpose:
This is a working notebook-style audit of how end-to-end latency 'onsets' (the shape of the latency distribution as requests transition from cold to warm execution modes) differ across model families, request shapes (prompt length and expected generation length), and batching configurations. Goal is to produce a compact playbook: metrics to monitor, dominant root-causes for tail events during onset windows, and low-risk mitigations to reduce p95/p99 during ramp periods (first N requests after container spinup, cache thrash, model swap).

Context / why this matters:
- We observe repeated p95/p99 spikes in production correlated with autoscale up events and model cutovers.
- These spikes disproportionately affect latency-sensitive routes (chat endpoints with streaming).
- Existing artifacts focus on steady-state p50/p95 (many docs), but operational pain happens during 'onset' windows when internal caches / GPUs / kernels are warming.

Dataset & instrumentation used:
- Traces: 48k end-to-end traces captured across 7 days (canary region us-west2). Each trace includes per-stage timestamps: ingress, tokenization, encode, kv-lookup, attention/compute, emit, postprocess, egress.
- Cohorts: by model (rw-base-7b, rw-chan-13b, rw-pt-70b), batch_size hint (1, 4, 8), seqlen groups (prompt <=64, 65-256, >256), and warm_state (cold: worker age < 30s or KV-miss rate > 80%; warm: worker age > 120s and KV-hit > 95%).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 of total e2e latency, and per-stage quantiles. Also measured: GPU kernel load, GPU SM utilization, NVLink counters, host CPU preemption stalls, and KV cache hit/miss heatmap.

Quick summary of findings:
1) Onset curve shape is model-dependent. Smaller models (7b) show a near log-linear tail rise for first 20 requests, dominated by kernel micro-warmups in compute stage. Large models (70b) show multimodal onset: an initial large p99 jump due to memory mapping + orchestra (paging/initialization) followed by smaller periodic spikes when sequence length expands.
2) KV cache warm misses create a secondary tail cluster at p95–p99 that persists longer than container age indicates. In practice, KV-hit ratio is a stronger predictor for p99 than worker age alone.
3) Batching interacts non-linearly: batch_size=8 reduces p50 substantially in warm state but increases p99 during onset because first coalesced batch waits for slower warming workers. "Straggler batches" amplify the tail.
4) Egress/emit stage is often underestimated: for streaming-enabled routes the incremental emit latency (first-token delay + token-emit jitter) contributed ~20% of p99 in small models when the runtime switched IO paths (sync->async) during warmups.

Representative numbers (example cohort summaries):
- rw-base-7b, prompt<=64, batch=1:
  - cold: e2e p50=110ms, p95=320ms, p99=680ms
  - warm: e2e p50=85ms, p95=130ms, p99=210ms
  - dominant cold-stage: compute kernel initial compile/hotpath + kv-miss
- rw-pt-70b, prompt>256, batch=4:
  - cold: e2e p50=720ms, p95=2.1s, p99=5.9s
  - warm: e2e p50=610ms, p95=780ms, p99=1.3s
  - dominant cold-stage: mmap/setup, attention kernel warmup, input staging to GPU

Root-cause hypotheses (ranked by impact):
- H1: Kernel caching/first-call compilation. Some backends JIT-select kernels at first request shapes, causing increased single-request compute time. Evidence: per-kernel invocation counts spike at onset; subsequent requests faster.
- H2: KV cache cold misses and eager refills. When a worker gets traffic for a new conversation, KV loader synchronously fetches/generates prefix states, blocking emit for that request.
- H3: Batcher coalescence stragglers. When workers with different warm states are grouped, the batch waits for slowest contributor.
- H4: Host-level IO stalls during model mmap (especially for large models on NFS).
- H5: Runtime path switches for streaming cause lock contention and increase emit jitter for small models

Actionable mitigations tested (short experiments):
- M1: Soft prewarm (asynchronous kernel probe): upon container start, run a lightweight probe with short synthetic prompts to force kernel selection; reduced p99 by ~35% on rw-base-7b. Low-risk and cheap.
- M2: KV prefetch window: when routing a conversation to a worker, if KV-hit < threshold, spawn a non-blocking prefetch thread that primes the KV; reduced the secondary tail cluster by ~60% in tests. Requires careful concurrency control.
- M3: Batch formation policy tweak: prefer homogeneous worker warm_state during coalescing; this reduced p99 for batch=8 by ~22% but increased drop in throughput in very high QPS bursts (trade-off).
- M4: NFS->local model cache policy: pin frequently-used model files locally on SSD for warm workers; significant benefit for >30B models in canary region but operational cost in storage.
- M5: Streaming path stability: avoid switching the IO path mid-request; keep streaming mode sticky per-worker until a stable warm threshold passes. Reduced emit jitter.

Proposed short-term rollout (next 6 weeks):
- Week 0-1: Run M1 as an opt-in feature for canary models. Track delta in p99 for first 1000 cold starts.
- Week 1-2: Implement KV prefetch prototype (M2) behind feature flag on dev environment; instrument contention metrics.
- Week 2-4: Add warm_state tag to batcher decision logic and experiment with homogeneous coalescing for low-latency routes only.
- Week 4-6: For 30B+ customers, test local-model-cache policy in a controlled region. Evaluate cost uplift vs latency benefits.

Monitoring and SLO changes suggested:
- Add "first-100s p99" metric per worker-model as a separate SLO KPI (we currently only measure rolling p99).
- Tag p99 spikes by onset-phase (container_age buckets) and KV-hit percent; this will help alert only on onset anomalies vs broad regressions.
- Add per-batch variance metric exposed in console: batch_size, batch_wait_ms_p95.

Open questions / next experiments:
- How stable are M1 gains across GPU generations (A100 vs H100) and with quantized kernels?
- Can we model/predict KV-miss cost per-conversation and surface a fallback (serve from smaller variant) automatically?
- Does service mesh sidecar (mTLS) handshake add measurable onset overhead in low-latency routes? Preliminary traces show ~5–10ms but worth quantifying under load.

Notes to reviewers:
- Raw trace export and analysis notebook referenced in linked_artifacts; feel free to pull cohort slices.
- This doc is a working audit — many hypotheses are fuzzy. I prefer iterating with small canary rollouts rather than big config flips.

Action items (who/when):
- Marco: prototype asynchronous kernel probe and measure p99 delta by 2024-11-27.
- Leah: wire the KV prefetch feature-flag and add telemetry for prefetch latency by 2024-12-04.
- Jen: add warm_state tagging to batcher and run A/B for low-latency routes by 2024-12-11.

Appendix (raw trace checklist):
- Ensure traces include per-stage timestamps with monotonic clock.
- Export KV hit/miss events per-request.
- Annotate container age, GPU serial, kernel versions, and model file checksum for each trace to enable grouping.

End of audit notes.

(Loose) Glossary: warm_state = worker age > 120s AND kv_hit_ratio > 95%; onset window = first 30s after worker creation or model swap.
